slides.title: The Philosophy of Religion
slides.question: Is there a God, and can reason tell?
slides.sub: Arguments for and against, faith and evidence, and traditions beyond the God of the philosophers
slides.notes:
Look up on a clear night far from city lights and you can see a few thousand stars of our galaxy, one of perhaps two trillion galaxies. Why is there something rather than nothing? Why is the universe the kind of place in which beings like us can ask that question?
Philosophy of religion asks whether reason can say anything about God: whether there are good arguments for God’s existence, good arguments against, and whether belief needs arguments at all. Believers, atheists and agnostics have all contributed, and the best work on each side takes the other seriously.
Next: what do we mean by ‘God’?

slides.title: The great traditions mean very different things by the ultimate
slides.sub: Before asking whether God exists, ask which ‘God’

items.caption: Classical theism
items.text: One personal God: all-powerful, all-knowing, wholly good (Judaism, Christianity, Islam)

items.caption: Tawhid
items.text: Islam’s radical oneness of God, beyond all likeness

items.caption: Brahman
items.text: Hindu traditions: ultimate reality, personal or impersonal

items.caption: The Dao
items.text: Daoism: the nameless way of nature, not a person

slides.bottom: Most arguments in Western philosophy concern the God of classical theism; other traditions ask different questions.
slides.notes:
The word God means very different things. The God of classical theism, shared by Judaism, Christianity and Islam, is a personal being who created the world and is all-powerful, all-knowing and perfectly good. Advaita Vedanta speaks of Brahman, ultimate reality, identical with the deepest self. Buddhism teaches liberation without any creator. Daoism speaks of the Dao, the way, which cannot be named. Spinoza identified God with nature itself.
Most of tonight’s arguments concern the God of classical theism, because that is where most of the argument has happened. But it is worth remembering that it is not the only conception.
Next: arguments from the existence of the universe.

slides.title: Why is there something rather than nothing? The cosmological argument
slides.sub: Al-Ghazali, Aquinas, Leibniz; William Lane Craig

challenge.title: The argument
challenge.text: Everything that begins to exist has a cause. The universe began to exist. So the universe has a cause, which must be beyond space and time.

answer.title: Leibniz’s version
answer.text: Even if the universe always existed, why does it exist at all? Every contingent thing needs an explanation; the explanation of everything contingent must be a necessary being.

open.title: Objections
open.text: Why must the cause be a personal God? Could the universe be a brute fact (Russell)? Does ‘cause’ even apply to time itself? And Buddhist and Humean thinkers deny we need a first cause at all.

slides.bottom: Even if the argument shows there is a first cause, a further step is needed to show it is God.
slides.notes:
The kalam argument, developed by medieval Islamic philosophers such as al-Ghazali and revived by William Lane Craig, says that whatever begins to exist has a cause, the universe began to exist, so it has a cause. Leibniz’s version doesn’t depend on a beginning: why is there anything at all, rather than nothing?
Critics such as Bertrand Russell replied that the universe might simply be there, a brute fact. And even if there is a first cause, more argument is needed to show it is a personal, good God.
Next: arguments from design.

slides.title: Design: does the order of the universe point to a designer?

a.name: The design argument
a.label: Paley · 1802 · fine-tuning
a.lead: Find a watch on a heath and you infer a watchmaker. Living things and the universe’s laws look designed too.
points: Physical constants fall in a narrow life-permitting range
Change some slightly, and no stars or chemistry

b.name: The replies
b.label: Hume · Darwin · multiverse
points: Many universes could make a life-friendly one likely
We could only observe a life-permitting universe anyway

slides.bottom: Darwin answered Paley about life; fine-tuning reopened the argument about physics.
slides.notes:
William Paley imagined finding a watch on a heath. Its parts fit together for a purpose, so we infer a watchmaker. Living things, he said, are far more intricate. Darwin’s theory of natural selection gave an alternative explanation of living design.
But modern physics has revived the argument. Several constants of nature seem finely balanced: alter them slightly and there would be no stable stars or chemistry. Is that evidence of design, of a multiverse in which every setting occurs somewhere, or of nothing at all, since we could only find ourselves in a universe that allows us?
Next: an argument that tries to prove God from the concept alone.

slides.title: The ontological argument tries to prove God from the idea of God alone

steps.title: Define
steps.text: God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived.

steps.title: Exists in the mind
steps.text: Even a doubter understands the idea, so God exists in the understanding.

steps.title: Greater in reality
steps.text: What exists in reality is greater than what exists only in the mind.

steps.title: So God exists
steps.text: Otherwise we could conceive something greater, which contradicts the definition.

slides.bottom: Kant’s reply: existence isn’t a property that makes a concept greater; it’s whether the concept is instantiated.
slides.notes:
Anselm’s argument has fascinated philosophers for nine hundred years because it seems to prove too much from too little. The monk Gaunilo replied at once: the same reasoning would prove a perfect island exists. Kant’s objection is the most famous: ‘existence is not a predicate’. Saying a thing exists doesn’t add a property to it; it says the concept applies to something.
Alvin Plantinga revived a modal version using possible worlds. Most philosophers, believers included, think it fails, but nobody agrees on exactly why.
Next: the strongest argument against God.

slides.title: If God is all-good and all-powerful, why is there so much suffering?

challenge.title: The problem
challenge.text: An all-powerful God could prevent suffering. An all-good God would want to. Yet earthquakes, disease and cruelty fill history.

answer.title: Theodicies
answer.text: Free will: a world with free creatures is better even if they choose evil (Plantinga). Soul-making: hardship builds courage and compassion (Hick). Sceptical theism: we can’t expect to see God’s reasons.

open.title: The hard cases
open.text: Natural evils that no free choice explains. Animal suffering over millions of years. A child dying in pain (Rowe’s fawn; Ivan Karamazov).

slides.bottom: The logical problem may be answered; the evidential problem, the sheer amount of suffering, is still hotly debated.
slides.notes:
The problem of evil is the most powerful argument against classical theism. The logical version says God and evil are flatly inconsistent; most philosophers now accept Plantinga’s reply that free will could make them consistent. The evidential version, pressed by William Rowe, is harder: think of a fawn burned in a forest fire, suffering for days with no one to learn from it. Does any purpose really require that?
John Hick argued the world is a place for ‘soul-making’, where character grows through struggle. Dostoevsky’s Ivan Karamazov replied that no future harmony could justify the suffering of one tortured child.
Next: does belief even need arguments?

slides.title: Does religious belief need evidence at all?
slides.sub: Four answers to the ethics of belief

cols.label: Evidentialism
cols.title: Proportion belief to evidence
cols.text: ‘It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence’ (Clifford, 1877).

cols.label: Pascal’s wager
cols.title: A bet worth making
cols.text: If God exists, belief gains infinitely; if not, little is lost. So bet on God.
cols.note: Problem: which God? Can you choose to believe?

cols.label: Reformed epistemology
cols.title: Properly basic
cols.text: Belief in God can be rational without argument, like belief in other minds (Plantinga).

cols.label: Fideism
cols.title: Faith beyond reason
cols.text: Faith is a passionate commitment, not a conclusion (Kierkegaard).

slides.bottom: The deepest disagreement may be not about evidence for God, but about whether evidence is the right standard.
slides.notes:
W. K. Clifford insisted that believing without sufficient evidence is always wrong. William James replied that some live, momentous choices can’t wait for evidence. Pascal offered a wager: the stakes are infinite, so believe. Alvin Plantinga argued that belief in God can be ‘properly basic’, rational without argument, the way your belief that other people have minds is. Kierkegaard went further: faith is a leap, and turning it into a probability calculation misunderstands it.
Next: religious experience.

slides.title: Religious experience
slides.sub: William James, The Varieties of Religious Experience, 1902
slides.caption: Can an experience be evidence?
slides.text: Millions report experiences of the divine. If we trust our senses about the world, should we trust such experiences too (Swinburne’s principle of credulity)? Or do conflicting religions and psychological explanations undermine them?
slides.notes:
William James studied religious experience as a psychologist and philosopher. Richard Swinburne’s principle of credulity says we should trust how things seem unless we have reason not to; if it seems to someone that God is present, that is some evidence. Critics reply that experiences in different traditions conflict, and that psychology and neuroscience can explain them. John Hick’s religious pluralism suggests that the great traditions are different human responses to one ultimate reality.
Next: the whole field on one page.

head: Argument
Supports
Main reply
rows: A first cause or necessary being
Brute fact; why a personal God?
Freedom needs distance; God isn’t hidden
slides.bottom: The arguments rarely settle the question alone; together they shape where the burden of proof lies.
slides.notes:
Here are the main arguments side by side, each with its best reply. Very few people change their minds because of a single argument. What arguments do is show what each side must explain.
Next: a toolkit.

slides.title: Four questions for any argument about God

steps.title: Which God?
steps.text: What exactly is being argued for or against?

steps.title: How far does it reach?
steps.text: Does it prove a first cause, a designer, or a loving God?

steps.title: What’s the alternative?
steps.text: What explains the same facts without God?

slides.bottom: Clarity about which God and which standard prevents most talking past each other.
slides.notes:
Four questions. Which God? How far does the argument reach? What is the rival explanation? And what standard of belief are we using? Most religious arguments go wrong because people disagree about one of these without noticing.
Next: what the field leaves us with.

slides.title: Philosophy of religion leaves us with the largest questions of all
questions: Why is there something rather than nothing?
Can suffering on this scale be part of a good world?
Must belief answer to evidence, or can it rest on trust?
slides.line: Believers and sceptics share one thing: these questions matter.
slides.notes: Whatever you believe, these are questions worth taking seriously. The best believers and the best sceptics have always done so.

slides.title: Discussion: bring the theory back to real life
questions: Can someone be good without believing in God?
Is it reasonable to believe something because it gives your life meaning?
Should schools teach arguments for and against religion?
slides.line: State the standard of belief you’re using first.
slides.notes: Three questions. Say first what standard of belief you are using: evidence, experience, or trust.
